utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there are no procedural issues to deal with, I would like to ask the Prosecution whether it's ready to call its next witness. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Mr. Alun Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Roberts into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher now hands out to you the solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Roberts. Mr. Roberts, you'll first be examined by Mr. Waespi, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: My full name is Alun Richard Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And please observe a pause between my questions and your answers, and you can look at the cursor that is moving in front of you on the screen and when it stops moving it's safe for you to start answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the witness could be given copies of his six witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, do you recall giving six witness statements to the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, Your Honours, these six witness statements have the following 65 ter numbers: The first one dates 27th August 1997, 65 ter 5320; the second statement dates 31st July 1998, 65 ter number 4811; the third statement, 28th February 2007, 65 ter number 4812; fourth statement, 7th February 2008, 65 ter number 4813; fifth statement, 4th March 2008, 65 ter number 4814; and the sixth statement, 2nd July -- in fact, it's dated 2nd July, but it was taken on the 30th June and 1st of July, 2008, 65 ter number 5321.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, did you have a chance to review these six statements before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I have reviewed them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do these statements accurately reflect your declarations on the matters covered?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: They reflect what I said at the time of making those statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do those statements accurately reflect what you would say if examined today on these matters here in court?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if these six statements could be tendered as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've forgotten one question, Mr. Waespi. The witness said: It reflects what I said. I would give the same answers, but whether they are truthful answers is not yet covered by your two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do these statements -- would these statements, are they truthful answers to what you were asked?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Thank you. I made them truthfully, and I declare that I still consider them to be made truthfully. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would not expect otherwise, but this is the series of questions and as covered now. If they were all lies, of course, that's not what I suggest in any way, then it would have been lies and it still be lies, which, of course, is not the purpose of this exercise. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If these six statements could be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, from your latest submission, I saw that, at least, there are no objections against admission of the 92 ter statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The only issue that I noted this morning, which I'm not sure if it's a mistake or not, but on the 5th, 6th, 7th February, 2008, there's a current occupation listed, and I wasn't sure if that was accurate or not. Perhaps Mr. Waespi can take a look. If it is, that's fine. I just thought for the purposes of clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, we'll go through them one by one. Witness statement 27th of August, 1997, would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P675.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P675 is admitted into evidence. Next one would be witness statement 31st of July, 1998 ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P676.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P676 is admitted into evidence. The third one is witness statement 28th of February, 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P677.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P677 is admitted into evidence. The supplementary witness statement dated the 7th of February, 2008 ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P678.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P678 is admitted into evidence. Next one 4 March 2008 ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P679.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P679 is admitted into evidence. And, finally, the further supplementary witness statement dated the 2nd of July, 2008 ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P680, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There are a number of exhibits that I'd like to tender. Given the objections by the Cermak Defence of three exhibits and by the Gotovina Defence of six exhibits, I suggest that during the course of my examination-in-chief, I'll be pulling up these six exhibits and lay a foundation with the witness and then we can argue of its admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, before putting something to the witness, I think there's also request to have them -- some of these documents to be added to the 65 ter list. Is there any objection against that as such, so apart from -- of course, you might say that if they can't be admitted, what's the use of putting them only the 65 ter list? But would that not be over formalistic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. That wasn't what I was going to say, Your Honour. I think, in our filing yesterday, we indicated that there are several that are duplicates. So I'm not sure if the Prosecution had a chance to review it and wishes to retender them or not. But other than that, no, Your Honour, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we proceed as follows. Mr. Waespi, have you looked at possible duplicates?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. The Cermak Defence and also the Gotovina Defence discovered that. Those 65 ter exhibits were already on our original list, and they don't need to be applied for again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if they're already on your list, no duplicates as far as documents sought to be admitted are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest that we proceed that we first hear the questions Mr. Waespi will put to the witness; that we'll finally deal with admission; and at once not to split them out, now deal with half of them and then the others ones. But those who were not contested there, we work on a basis of the assumption that they will be admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, can you very briefly give a summary of your professional background and experience prior to your assignment in the United Nations force in the Krajina. I see from your February 2008 statement, which is now P678, that you were in South Africa. That's at page 2, paragraph 5. Can you briefly, very, very briefly, summarize your experience.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I was not so much in South Africa. I was working in my former profession as a journalist for two agencies, and I was covering the war in northern Namibia, which was then occupied by South African defence forces, and the war in southern Angola. And I worked for a correspondent for a news agency called the Namibian, based in Windhoek, the capital of Namibian, as well as research for the UK Manchester-based TV station, KRNA Television, for its world and action programme on a documentary about the war in southern Angola. And I covered that period about between 1985 and 1989, and it gave me an opportunity to see the grim realities of war first-hand as a correspondent, including a range of activities between military and civilian locations. I think that sums that up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts. Now, did you also work for the ICC, International Criminal Court, here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I had a post as a senior public information officer from about the 2nd of August, last year, to the end of last year prior to them assigning a full-time spokesperson. And my assignment was on policy making regarding the responsibilities and conduct of court officials in regard to talking to the media, public speaking engagements, and those kind of policy directives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts. Let's turn to the events you came to testify about, and we'll start with the events in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could go and pull up witness statement 31st July 1998, which is now P676, at page 4, paragraph 3. And in B/C/S, it's page 5 in the middle. If the English version -- yes. Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll read out a few lines from the middle of the English version where it starts: "From those observations ..." That's the third paragraph. "From those observations, I estimate that about 200 civilian locations were hit during the shelling ..." And that, of course, refers to the events in Knin on the 4th and 5th of August, 1995. "This would include roofs of apartment buildings and houses that were hit or suffered damage from shrapnel, from the shelling, shattered windows, et cetera. "That the shelling affected the whole length of Knin, I observed four separate civilian buildings at either end of the town and in the middle of the town (on which a large amount of shelling was concentrated) as a further indication that the shelling was not just concentrated on military and official building locations of the 'RSK' authorities." And then you go on to describe at least four civilian locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If 65 ter number 5330, this is a map, could be pulled up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Roberts, the first four locations marked with H, L, K -- H, I, K, and L, are these those four civilian buildings you observed being shelled?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Just let me take a really good look to be really sure the map coincides with everything, but could you just put the picture as it is on the screen so I can see the actual list of -- right. Yes. Those are the four locations that I observed that I said in that statement, for me, depict the shelling affected was the word I used, "affected," the entire town of Knin H, I, L -- H, I, K, and L.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where were you when you made these observations?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I was in my UN public information white UN vehicle. I had seen these amongst other locations in patrols since we were able to have freedom of movement in the centre of Knin. And I made these sightings in regard to different locations in Knin, probably towards about the 17th or the latter part of August, as being just representing a focus of the happenings of the shelling and the bombardment that took place on the 4th and the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this photo could be tendered, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P681.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P681 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could move on to the next 65 ter, that's just the following number, 5331, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while that's being done, can you tell the Trial Chamber where you were during the shelling on the 4th, on the 5th? It's contained in the various witness statements, just very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, when the first bombardment of Knin commenced at about 5.00, I was in my apartment accommodation on the top floor of a building just off from the centre of Knin. Most of the detail of what happened is explained in my statement. I left there after being assisted by a UN armoured patrol carrier. At about 8.40, we were taken by Canadian peacekeepers in the APC to other parts of Knin up and along towards the police station and the former so-called RSK military barracks to pick up other people on the main road. We then collected them and returned back down the main road past the centre of town along to the Krka river and into the UN Sector South compound. I was there for some days and nights following.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Roberts. I think that suffices for the moment because we are focusing on the shelling of Knin. Now, on this map -- or rather, photo, we see A, accommodation. Is that your accommodation as you had described just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, that is. That white speck building on the corner of the road there, that was my accommodation in Knin at the time of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the other locations depicted here in the map and explained in the legends, what do these mean?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Let's take those slowly one by one. The capital B with the line running across the photo there is an apartment block building that was directly visible in front of my top floor balcony of my accommodation. The top parapet of that building I saw damaged when I could get up to the balcony after the main bulk of shelling had subsided. After about one and a quarter hours, I saw that it had an impact. B1 denotes the body of a man I saw lying on the sidewalk. C is the building to the right of the road running directly opposite from my balcony. It was a house more than an apartment block, as I think can be seen from the photo, and I saw smoke rising from the far right-hand corner of that building. D is a building which I could see from the front edge looking to the right of my balcony, but I would ask the Court to remember there is a considerable elevation that goes up from my building and from the railway line and the main road in Knin going up towards the fortress. So I couldn't see completely clearly the roof-top depicted on the image there, D. But when looking carefully at maps and sketches of maps, that is the building where I saw smoke rising from the top far side of the roof. Going to E, now in my statement of 1998, I describe how I was lying in the centre part of the accommodation building on the second floor with the family I was staying with and that I heard shells going over the top of our building at a kind of slight angle. Obviously, then, I couldn't see them, but they appeared to be going to the back and up. And this is only my assessment of where those shells might have fallen, but I've labelled it as E. Now, F is the body of a woman. It's on the street to my right, which I could see from the corner of the balcony, who was lying face down. G is something on this symbol as labelled third body; but in my statement, it's at the end of the street, beyond the house which is labelled C that I saw having damage. And I could not be sure at all because of the distance - it's about 80 metres, a bit more perhaps - if this was a body or not. So I have not in my actual statement said it was. It could have been but I wasn't sure because of that distance balcony top of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts. Just to make it clear, at what time, on which date did you observe those points you just made?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: It would be the morning of the 4th of August after I had got up on the balcony to make some assessments. It was after the shelling had died down at about half past 6.00 onwards. I can't be precisely sure, but it was a little bit after the main bulk of shelling had subsided. It was not, by the way, for the Court just one visit to the top of the balcony to look. I made several visits in the course of maybe half an hour or 45 minutes where I could make observations, detect maybe a little bit about the rate of impact of shelling coming in, which had subsided at that time, after about an hour and a quarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this photo could be tendered, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P682 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If P -- if 65 ter number 5329 could be brought up. This is a larger collection of photographs, and I would like to see first page 3 and then page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, can you tell us what is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: It would be useful to have a map to help the Court perhaps, but I can describe it quite well. I think it's also on a map we might see later. If you go up from the main street just after the so-called RSK government buildings, you climb a very steep elevation, and you're going up the road away from the centre of town opposite what was the so-called super-market at that time. And you go up steeply, and you reach some concrete steps on the road that goes around to the right, but you climb upwards directly. You come to a dirt road at that time, and you turn to your left. As you're going left you on both sides have civilian buildings, bungalows most of them. And this building here, if you're walking along - if I can help the Court to imagine - if you're walking along from the top of those steps, you've gone about a hundred metres, maybe less. You can see two buildings on the dirt road. The balcony on the left-hand side is the edge of one building. You can see an impact in the roof of that building, which I felt was accommodation building, top roof was hit. And I made the observation that this was some distance away from the centre of town; and as I reflected elsewhere in the statements, I felt it to be beyond what I would observe to be legitimate military objects. It's the top end of town away from the centre up the elevation climbing towards civilian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts. We'll show you a map in a moment. Let's go to the next photo --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'd like to tender all these 31 photos that are part of this 65 ter number 5329 at the end of having discussed two examples, if that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we know whether there will be any objections, because then you might choose --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I do have a -- I don't think it's been disclosed, the foundation for the pictures in particular at the time they were taken. I notice the lack of leaves on the trees, so if we could have some foundation as to when the pictures were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi, if you could please deal with that for the whole series of photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I will certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, these photographs, who took these photographs, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I took these photographs, and I think it's a fair question. They were taken later on. I took some photographs in late August/early September. These were taken -- these particular photographs we're looking at now were taken probably towards the late part of September/early October maybe. This particular building is on the same dirt road. If you recalled the building we just saw a moment ago, it's about 30 metres to the left of that building. This building is just down from the dirt road; and if you went beyond that roof and turn right a little bit, you come to the steps, concrete steps, that go down to the street and then down the street into the centre of town. It was a civilian accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And for everybody's benefit, the witness explained the date these pictures were taken and the locations in his witness statement, the last one, which is now P680, on the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that sufficiently deal with the foundation matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, if I could have a moment, Your Honour. Is there a paragraph number, Counsel, that you could give me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, 32. It starts in the second-to-the-last page and finishes discussing each of the photographs on the last page of P680.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the location -- I'm sorry to ask these questions. But in light of the fact that we've had the map -- the first map admitted into evidence as to where the witness says he saw damage to civilian buildings, is this -- are these now different locations; and if so, are these pictures of buildings below the Knin castle?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. I wanted to use a map once these photos are dealt with, go back to map P681. We can do that, and the witness can indicate, as he suggested, where these photographs were taken. But if the Defence is satisfied, if these photos can be moved into evidence. We can also go back to the map right now, Mr. President, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Still the -- we are talking about the photographs dealt with in paragraph 32?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is correct of the last witness statement dated 30 June -- 31st July 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let me just see. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt you, bit I also note that the -- it says the date the photos are taken is 18 August 1995, which would seem to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm struggling a bit also with the dates because the witness said, "We're looking at these pictures of these two buildings," and you said, "These photographs, who took them?" And the witness said, "I took some in late August/early September." And then ... Yes, Mr. Waespi, about the dates, I do not see any photograph on this list. I see one from mid-October, that's the cemetery, which apparently is not the one we have on our screen. And all the others are either August or early September. Now, I'm not familiar with the seasons there. Would that have been early September?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, in your witness statement, you say that, in paragraph 32, that it was taken around the 18th August 1995. Do you want to qualify this answer?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I can do. I mean, I was taking photographs from quite shortly after Operation Storm, and I took a good many -- I had taken photographs in that same dirt road about that time. These may be, on reflection, been taken -- these specific ones may have been taken in the later part of September, but they clearly were buildings I observed. And whether the photographs on that dirt road were taken in August, maybe that's part of the confusion. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not very familiar with how leaves look at the end of September in Knin, but I'm -- to say the least, I'm a bit surprised by it. Mr. Roberts, we see some vegetation which has a look. And if we go through the series, then I think it's always one photograph followed by a number page. If we then, in this series, would go to the second photograph, we've seen that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two and three, I think, Your Honour, on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Two and three appears -- at least in many countries in the world, this looks like late autumn, not one single leaf left on the trees. And in the back, we see some green, but I can't identify whether that is leaf trees or needle trees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, certainly they were taken by me, and the date could be something towards the end of September. But I don't know how it could be taken much into October because I was transferred from Knin around the middle of October, so I don't think I would concur that they were taken somehow in the -- in the early/mid/deep winter. They were taken certainly no later than the end of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's, of course, a conclusion saying, Since I wasn't there anymore, the photographs couldn't be from that date, or these are different photographs, or -- I mean, you are at this moment in the process of drawing conclusions rather than to identify --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did take these photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did take them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did take these photographs, and the description I've given is accurate, and the latest date I could have taken them would be towards the end of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not return after that date to the place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned, yes, but not to this place to take photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to tender these 30 documents -- photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the position that we believe that this is beyond October --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, that's also --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to some extent speculation. So if -- well, I wouldn't say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- wild speculation, Mr. Misetic, but at least it's also based on assumptions which have not yet been verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, this document which is a series of, I think, 31 photographs --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and 62 pages of photographs separated by numbers coming after the photograph would be number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit Number P683, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P683 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Roberts, if we can go back to the map P681, and I'd like to ask you to mark on this map, if you can, the location of these two houses you just described a moment ago, if Madam Usher could assist you in doing that.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: How do you move the cursor? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. You have to be a little bit patient. Madam Usher is coming to help you.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you can please mark those two houses we've seen on those two photographs. If you recall the first one, that should be the first one, and you would attach once you have found it a number 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: They're on the dirt road --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would it assist if the image would be --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- larger, zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: The buildings are quite -- the buildings are quite close together where the letter K is on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think you can also describe it using K -- in fact, the circle that depicts the location of K as your reference point.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I think it's not easy from this map in the way that the circle around K is drawn. This is the edge of the dirt road that runs along the top, and it's a very, very small road and it's not picked out clearly on this whole diagram or sketch map. But the two buildings were close together around whereabout the circle marked K is. That is the area of those two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. I don't think you need to mark it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I don't think we need a new exhibit. We just leave it as P681.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now if we can continue, all these locations, were these civilian locations or what you perceived at that time as military facilities, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I consider these to be civilian locations, civilian accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts. Let's move on to -- away from the shelling and to other observations you made. In your witness statement, the second one, 31st of July, 1998, which is now P676, you made the following observation. And I quote from page 1, paragraph 3; in B/C/S, it's also the first page. "During the course of the 'Operation Storm' attack on Knin, my job was to represent the United Nations observations of what we, the HQ Sector South UN personnel, saw taking place. And to continue doing that over the weeks that followed were a consistent pattern of orchestrated arson, systematic looting, on what I would describe as a mass scale, and many incidents of deliberate killing and murder took place. The latter on many occasions from the bodies I observed personally, sometimes within hours of the incidents, were elderly people, all of which were dressed in civilian clothes." Now, on what basis did you make this comment in your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I made that statement from my presence in Knin on the 4th of August of what I observed then, but especially in regard to my own personal presence with members of the United Nations Human Rights Action Teams visiting many villages and hamlets in the outlying areas around Knin, as well as a wider area of the former Sector South as we began to get greater and better freedom of movement. I also, as the public information officer, was privileged to have all of the reports in my office from the four UN battalions, KenBat, CanBat, CzechBat, and JorBat information officers in the sector; all of the daily situation reports of the United Nations military observers; the daily sitreps of the UN civilian police; the Human Rights Action Team reports; the military information officer's reports; as well as the reports of the humanitarian and political affairs officers who were, all of them, at various points out in the field on a regular, daily basis from after the 8th of August. I referred to those reports as well as what I also saw personally in making that description here in the 1998 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to 65 ter 5324, which is a PIO report of 12th October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, do you recognise this document; and if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this document. This is a document that I prepared myself on -- dated 12th of August, but I prepared it maybe a week or ten days before. And what it is intended to do is to bring together in one place, for us as a public information department and my colleagues in the mission headquarters in Zagreb, a representation of what is contained or what was contained in the various UN reports of UNMOs, UN Human Rights Action Teams, UNCIVPOL, and others, of where they'd seen really and seen personally and where they said, We saw, I saw, acts of serious human rights violations conducted by members of the Croatian army or people in military uniform which the UN personnel concluded were Croatian army soldiers or personnel. And the whole report is a selection. There were more, but I thought were representative of the descriptions and the work done especially by UNCIVPOL. And just briefly, I chose UNCIVPOL because their reports were quite descriptive with a grid reference and also because maybe I was completely wrong but I felt that it was possible maybe some part of UNCIVPOL might continue after the finalisation of the UNCRO mandate, which did not happen. But I relied upon their reports especially. And in their reports, as well as the UN action teams, the latter part of that report includes summaries of interviews mostly by UNCIVPOL with civilians who said to UN people what they had seen and saw, and then showed UNCIVPOL and UN human rights personnel various evidence of serious or violent human rights situations that we thought credible. Each one of the references in the report, I have sourced with the particular UNCIVPOL or UN Human Rights Action Team or UN UNMO report from which I looked and read the information before setting down the various paragraphs representing what the UN have seen in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts. Let's turn to page 2, and we see here quite a number of international journalists. I'd like to ask you first: Have you seen -- have you worked with at that time in the Knin area with all these journalists that are listed here?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: This is a selection of the many international and regional press who came through our press office to either use the equipment, computers, sometimes to type stories, to request assistance in meeting UN personnel who might give them information, and sometimes request assistance of perhaps accompanying UN personnel on their trips into the field, especially UN Human Rights Action Team and UNMOs and CIVPOL. I met with almost all these people, they passed our office, they are amongst -- they are a selection of many more international and local press.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm interested in two names. The first one is Robert Fisk, he's listed here under Independent newspaper UK, 3 September; and Christiane Amanpour, CNN, 2nd October. In relation to Mr. Fisk, when do you recall having met with him, if you have, indeed, met with him?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Robert Fisk came several times to report on the situation in Sector South and Croatia. He was there maybe a few weeks before this, but he'd come back and was there from about eight to ten days from just before, I think, the 3rd of September. And he went out into the villages around Knin and produced, I think, three or four reports for the Independent, which is a newspaper based in London, UK. Ms. Amanpour had also been in Sector South previously. Like Robert Fisk, she was covering the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina especially, but she made several trips into Croatia and Sector South. And that date there is the date that she was in our office. But these dates on the right are just the date that I put down that they were in the office. They were coming and going quite frequently. Some of them -- others made maybe just one visit on the way through.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this document could be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P684.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P684 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I would like to play a tape which is a news report by Christiane Amanpour for CNN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a video, may I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It's a four-minute video which has a transcript. It was given to, I think, the interpreters, and I believe Mr. Kay has an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's a broad-ranging objection in relation to this particular piece of evidence as well as the Fisk articles. These are, of course, reports by other people, not this witness. This witness may have known the people, he may have known that they were in the area at the time. But the observations and report are particular and peculiar to those journalists who are the ones writing the material or, in this case, producing the news report. I cannot understand the admissibility of material such as that because one can easily see that a witness such as this or any other witness could then be used as a vehicle to bring through whatever newspaper reports containing the observations and thoughts of other journalists to suit whatever purposes a particularly -- particular party has within these proceedings. In my submission, the evidence the Court must receive is this witness's own observations, what he saw, what he heard, and keep it to that. To produce materials from people who are in some way connected to him and then put them into evidence, in my submission, doesn't provide this Court with a satisfactory means of receipt of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe, first of all, these documents and videos have a value of their own as a piece of notice, general notice, that was aired or published. We could actually submit them from the bar table, but the witness himself, as is reflected in his witness statements, had contacts with these two journalists. He met with Mr. Fisk. He actually accompanied him to one of the tours in Kistanje and Djevrska, and you'll see that when we pull up the article. So he adds, clearly, a foundation to these articles because he was there and he talked to the journalist. In relation to the CNN clip, Mr. Roberts even features in the CNN clip. He was interviewed by Christiane Amanpour, so we believe that there is enough foundation to tender these media articles with Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, the objection is denied. As Mr. Waespi rightly pointed out, if the witness was involved in one way or the other in the production or was present during the production, he can say something about it, which does not mean that everything that is said and is photographed or is described is necessarily the ultimate truth. But under the circumstances, as presented by Mr. Waespi, there -- the general objection as phrased by you is denied. But, of course, we'll first now have a look at the material, and then finally decide on admission. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If 65 ter number 5333 video could be played, and it lasts approximately four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Unknown present: "The three sides in the Bosnian conflict have been accused of committing atrocities, all of them at one time. Today, the Croats have been singled out for mistreating the Serbs in the Krajina. The UN high commissioner for human rights has written Croatia's President Tudjman, accusing his forces of continued killing in Krajina. CNN's Christiane Amanpour has an example. Christiane Amanpour: "UN soldiers show journalists what they found in the tiny village of Varivode a few days earlier. Unknown soldier: "We got blood-stains on the floor, we got two entries wounds from rifle bullets or pistol in there, and then another set of stains over the corner here. Christiane Amanpour: "UN soldiers say an elderly Serb couple lived here. The man was sick in bed-ridden. Below their picture hanging on the bedroom wall, we found a dog crouching in the corner as if in mourning. The soldiers believe the owners of this house were executed. Unknown soldier: "It's obvious that it wasn't shot from the entrance but from here. The bullet-holes like this [indiscernible]. Christiane Amanpour: "We saw the same pattern in several nearby homes, blood-stains on the ground, a cane lying nearby, a bullet-hole in the wall, abandoned farm animals. 74-year-old Milan Pocrajec, a Serb, is the only one left in this village. He says he heard the shooting, but he didn't see anything and now he's terrified. Milan Pocrajec: [B/C/S spoken] Christiane Amanpour: "If they come and want to kill me, I can't do anything, he says. I can't go anywhere. The UN believes 12 Serb civilians were massacred in Varivode, among them Jovo and Milka Beric. According to identity papers they found, their bodies have been buried along with more than 200 others who were killed during and after the Croatian army retook the Krajina from the Serbs in August. One hundred twenty-five of these graves are unmarked. At first, Croatian authorities denied the reports attributing them to biassed propaganda. Later, they blamed 'uncontrollable elements' and now they say they've arrested several hundred people. The UN says what's happening here is a systematic campaign of intimidation. Varivode is only the latest destroyed village. UN television has taken pictures of Serb houses burning all over this region in the two months since the Croatian army conquered it. UN cameras found two elderly Serb men, one dressed in pajamas shot through shot through the head, the other with his throat slit. European, UN, and US human rights reports say much of the killing, burning, and looting is done by men in Croatian military uniforms and armed civilians. The US has protested. John Shattuck: " ... of these abuses need not have occurred on this scale if the Croatian government had taken measures to prevent them ... Christiane Amanpour: "Officially, Croatia says, Serbs who have lived in the Krajina region for hundreds of years can stay, but the signals say others. Alun Roberts: "We're seeing repeated signs of burning, looting, and killing of the remaining civilians. There is no sign of any encouragement for those people to stay or for those who may have left to come back in any way at all. Christiane Amanpour: "And as UN soldiers leave, they promise to come back and see Milan ... [overlapping speakers]. Christiane Amanpour: "If you you find me alive, he says, if you find me alive. Christiane Amanpour, CNN, Varivode, Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like this tender this video-clip, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further observations, apart from the ones raised by Mr. Kay? Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P685.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P685 would then include the video and the transcript. P685 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me go back to the two articles by Mr. Fisk. The first one is 65 ter number 963.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the article, Mr. Roberts, talks about in the first paragraph visits by Mr. Fisk to Kistanje and Djevrska. Did you accompany Mr. Fisk to these locations?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: On that occasion, yes, I was with Robert Fisk when he made that report in Kistanje and Djevrska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to tender this article, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections, other than the one further raised by Mr. Kay? If not, Madam Registrar, this would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P686, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P686 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the next potential exhibit is 65 ter 5334.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, that's an article dated 14th September 1995, again by Mr. Fisk. And it features in the filled of the first page a Lieutenant Simon Coley, and also at another location an Irish UN investigator, just in the paragraph below, Bridin O'Rourke. Are you familiar with these two persons, Mr. Coley and Bridin O'Rourke?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Mr. O'Rourke worked in the CIVPOL HQ office in Sector South Knin, and Lieutenant Coley was an UNMO attached to UN military observers in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know how Mr. Fisk got in touch with these two UN persons?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: As I recall, what I would not all the time do, but have the possibility to do, would be to have journalists go in the field with some of our UN Human Rights Action Teams where I would not be present. On this occasion, I recall that Mr. Fisk was there during this visit doing his reports, and they were going out in the field, Lieutenant Coley and CIVPOL lady, and O'Rourke. I inquired from them, Could a journalist go with them. Fisk was interested, and he went with them on that occasion. I did not accompany them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am told that neither this document or the CNN video-clip are on the 65 ter, nor has an application been made to add them to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I omitted that. I would like to add those to the 65 ter list. We received these documents only -- I believe we received the CNN clip from Mr. Roberts when he visited us I think about three weeks ago, and the article by Mr. Fisk, the second one, we pulled out of the system around the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no date I can see on this article either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's 14th September 1995, the second article. The first one I believe was the 4th September 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what you believe is, of course, good to know, but not the ultimate. Yes, September 14th, 1995, apparently that's, at least, what seems to be the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can see, Your Honour, on the bottom of the first page of this document, it appears to have been printed on July 10th, 2008. So, at least, it's been in someone's possession since that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you said, that you then received it from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Because the witness showed us that document dated 12th October 1995, which is P684, which features on page 2 of Mr. Fisk; and after that, we tried to find the articles Mr. Fisk wrote at that time and presented it to Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other potential problem I have with this is that how do we cross-examine? I mean, there is no notation in this article that Mr. Roberts was interviewed or quoted. I mean, how do we cross-examine someone on an article in which they weren't quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, again, as Your Honour has said a moment ago, the witness facilitated the visit of the gentleman. Obviously, the journalist made his own observations. He's a reputable journalist. The document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly the problem Mr. Misetic and now apparently Mr. Kuzmanovic are raising. If written statements, articles speak for themselves, what's the use of asking questions about it, isn't it? What questions would you ask about this in examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we had so many documents that were authored by another person than the witness who tendered these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's always the problem with these documents if the author is different from the witness. That's as far as it goes. Of course, it goes to the value attached to a document like that, if the author can be cross-examined. Of course, nobody prevents the Defence from calling Mr. Fisk, and we would certainly not be opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. This now opens the door to everybody going to Lexus Nexus, finding all the newspaper articles they want, and tendering them into evidence as evidence, and then telling the other side, Go call the journalist to cross-examine them. I mean, at some point, there has to be a line drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I can't say that I've never seen a document coming from the Defence in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Only if the -- I mean, as far as I can recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- if the witness is quoted in the article, then putting it to him to say, Did you say this on the day in question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have seen other examples as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I totally understand and I do agree with you, but I think you have to realize that we got a CD of some 800-some documents produced in our lockers. I don't know. I haven't looked at every single page and I can't tell you if this was included in that. But this is the first I've seen of this particular article. I understand Your Honour's position, that confronting people with articles or giving them articles in direct with which we had perhaps previous contact with and had a chance to prepare is one thing. But the difficulty with this particular witness is there's so much information, and every week we get a new statement or new supplemental information sheet or information that wants to be added to the 65 ter which obviously hasn't been added. I understand Mr. Waespi has this witness and there's a lot of information and documentation. But for us to effectively cross this person, you know, there has to be sort of an end as to when we get the documents, and it hasn't happened here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, it appears to me, but please correct me when I understand the Defence wrongly, that this witness has drafted a list of some 20 journalists he has met at the time, facilitated, could use the computer, sometimes were accompanied and sometimes were not accompanied. Now, it seems of some concern to the Defence that if you would admit into evidence every single written report about what these journalists apparently have seen without supporting pictures or without any additional information about who accompanied him, we've seen Mr. Roberts featuring on one of the clips. So, at least, he could tell us whether he was there; and whether this was the journalist who made it and whether the environment in which he was videoed, whether that was authentic or not. I mean, he can say a bit more, but this would open a way to every written report about the events by any of these witness -- by these journalists, just on the basis that they'd visited the offices, to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are just two examples, including the CNN three examples, of what the witness described a regular occurrence, that international journalists would come. It serves as an example as a corroboration of what the witness told us, especially in P684, and these are one- and two-page articles. Obviously, if the Defence cannot cross the author, that goes to the value of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if the Independent was translated into Croatia at the time. I mean, if Mr. Waespi is seriously going down this route, he has to present it in a proper and effective way. I was trying to alert the Court at the start to what I could see as a bridgehead approach by the Prosecution in relation to this kind of material, and it's become more and more transparent to me that that is what is going on here. Looking at the Amanpour clip, it looked to me as though that was several different places edited together. I'm not sure it is of just the one place, and I'm not sure how the Court will be helped by edited information as well as the views of journalists coming into this Tribunal in that way. There must be some connection with the accused or with the witness himself, rather than the views and observations of other parties. That's our concern at the bar here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether or not to admit the Roberts/Fisk report will be decided after the break by the Chamber. But, Madam Registrar, could you perhaps already mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P687, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before I forget and I wanted to put it on the record with respect to the Amanpour clip in light of the conversation we had earlier, when she was standing in the cemetery, the trees were full of leaves. So I wanted to note that for the record in light of our discussion, and that clip had to be at least the 2nd of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That says something about the seasons, you would say, yes. Mr. Waespi, perhaps you could also over the break look again not only at the second and the third in this series of photographs but also to the fourth, where you see something which some people would -- no, let me not comment on it. The witness said the second and the third might be problematic. If you could please have a close look at fourth as well. Please, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's continue -- unless, Mr. President, I'm moving on to a different subject. That's a lists of human rights violations which I probably cannot deal in the next three minutes but I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you cannot. Could you tell us in how much time you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps in -- well, maybe I'll try in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes. Then we'll finish that and then we'll then take a break until 11.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If 65 ter 5326 could be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While that's being done, do you remember Judith Jakob?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was she?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Judy Jacob was my press and public information assistant in the press and public information office in Sector South headquarters in Knin, and she had arrived in Sector South headquarters a few months before I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at the cover page of this list, and once you have familiarized yourself, we can move on to the section page, which is the first page of the actual list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' benefit, this is an almost identical copy the actual list of P421 that was admitted after some debate with Mr. Kehoe with Witness Marti. And do you recall that Mr. Marti said that two of the columns were cut off. If we could move to the second page of this document, please, and if that could not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this list is, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There are, in fact, two lists which are identical. One is dated the 29th of November, as I recall, and one is not dated. The undated one, as I recall, is the official one that we circulated to certain members of mission headquarters in Zagreb, as well as the heads of some of the Sector South departments. What this report is, as our public information office would do on some occasions - I think the Court is familiar but I will just make sure - that in the course of a UN mission anywhere in the world, the different departments, such as was in Sector South, the UN military observers, the UNCIVPOL, UN human rights action teams, sector commander's office, all the departments would file at the end of each day a situation report or a daily sitrep. In the course of the weeks that followed, from the 4th of August on through towards the end of the UNCRO mission in November, that pattern continued. The press office was, therefore, receiving all of these reports, and our observation was that there was nowhere in Sector South, nor as far as we knew, at mission headquarters Zagreb that had brought together a comprehensive document to list as best we could all of the reporting of the different UN sitreps and daily reports, to have them in a chronological order based upon the sightings and the reports made by UN personnel. And therefore, we decided with the consent of the UN departments in Sector South to be the office that would put this together. So we did this from the 4th of August onwards to the middle of November, and we finished this up in the mission headquarters in Zagreb, as I recall, in early January. The role of Judith Jacob was largely to bring together all of these different reports. We would discuss them when I came in from field trips in the evening, and gradually we built-up this ledger of tables and information that was inserted. And we tried to be as thorough as possible based upon the content of information provided in these UN reports, which she and I would go to the personnel concerned and ask them to on occasion to verify or be clear on information that they had written in their report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this list could be tendered, under seal, because it contains a few names of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if just for the record we could get the foundation as to where the document actually came from. I mean, to the Office of the Prosecutor, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- this specific document was given to us by Mr. Roberts. That's the first time we've seen the complete list with those two columns at the far right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you could inquire as to where he got it from. I think there's a little bit of background there, just as the foundation for the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe the witness just testified that he compiled the document with Ms. Jacobs together, but we can clarify that with Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't mind. The document was compiled by Ms. Jacob and myself with the cooperation of the various members of the other UN units. I was advised that one of your earlier witnesses, Mr. Marti, had said, apparently, that he had received this document from Ms. Judith Jacob, and I was contacted then to ask about this document. I found the original of it, which is the undated document, and delivered this to the investigators of ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding based on communication with the Prosecution that Ms. Jacobs is actually the one who's providing this document, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can go back to my e-mail which I sent a memo to everybody, and I'm quite confident we did not receive the list from Ms. Jacobs, but for the first time from Mr. Roberts. But I'll verify that over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are referring at this moment to an e-mail which was copied to the Chamber, dated the 23rd of June of this year, three minutes past 7.00 in the afternoon. Is that correct, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And I have it in front of me right now, and in it, Mrs. Jacobs says at page 2, the top, that she did not have a copy of the list anymore. So that confirms that she didn't give us the list herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P688, in the absence of objections, is admitted into evidence. We'll have a break now, Mr. Roberts, until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, when we were discussing P688 and when it was admitted into evidence, I have failed to mention that it was admitted under seal. Then as far as P687 is concerned, that is the newspaper article of a -- apparently dating from the 14th of September. The Chamber has considered that in more than one respect the document does not meet the criteria for being admitted at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go back, as suggested by you, Mr. President, to P683, which is the series of 30 photographs, and I'm interested in page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I recall I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what does it depict?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: It was one of many photographs. It wasn't taken specifically to show what's in the picture, but it depicts general decay and looting in the streets towards the upper part of town in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What's very particular I think about this photo is the very white foreground. Do you have an explanation for that as the photographer?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yeah, I see it also. I don't have any specific information to that. I know I took the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Waespi. Are you telling us this depicts looting? Is that what I heard? I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's -- I think the testimony is such, unless there's any translation issues, seems to be clear. Whether it's for you very convincing, Mr. Kuzmanovic, you can, of course, tell the Chamber at a later stage. But before we start talking about the white, Mr. Roberts, is this snow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not like to go and say clearly or not. What I can say is I most certainly took this photograph. The selection of it for the purposes of suggesting looting is not my decision, but I submitted this photograph with many others, and I think it's before the Court, for what it's worth, to show what is in front of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, the first thing and the reason why I ask specific attention is that if it would be late September, then it would have been in -- if this is snow and if this would have been late September, it would have been in early winter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I follow you, yes. I can't give any more information than that. I don't recall taking the photograph in side-streets in Knin in the middle of the winter. I can't recall that. I can recall taking this photograph, but not that far into a season of winter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, of course, it's part of a series. If it would not have been, I would have invited you to reconsider the probative value and the relevance of this photograph. Now, to take it out of a series, I mean, if you would -- I leave it in your hands at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it raises more questions than it answers apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not a photographer, not even an amateur one. I was wondering whether the flash-light could have been the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I, of course, had similar considerations, but then, of course, further down on some of the branches, you find tiny little parcels of flash-light. I can't exclude anything, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We'll do away with this photograph, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to the second list, and, Mr. President, this list did not appear on the 65 ter -- on our current 65 ter list. So we need to apply, and there was also some objections from both Defence teams. So I would like to first lay a foundation with this witness, and this is ter 3150.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, do you recognise this list?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: This is a list that I was given by a UN military observer, and I understand, at the time it was given to me, I did not know who was the producer of the document. The information it contained is a summary, as far as I could tell at the time and now, of UN reports from different departments, which on the far right columns of the article you're looking at, source of information says the source of information. It doesn't give specific dates of the sitreps, but I understand it was actually prepared by Ms. Peggy Hicks, who was a colleague. She was one of the United Nations human rights officers based at mission headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you use this list in your daily activities?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I referred to this list in the course of compiling the 12th of October report that I put together myself, but only in terms of just looking at the descriptions and the dates as the way that various happenings, various incidents unfolded in Sector South around Knin from the 4th of August onwards. There was another report which covered also Sector North, and I used this in giving a guidance to my obtaining and checking the information in my 12th of October report of the specific situation reports of UNCIVPOL and UNMOs which are sourced in the 12th of October document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Based on the witness's answer, Mr. President, I'd like to make an oral application to add it to the 65 ter list and to have it tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two requests. First, adding to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my assistant here tells me that it's already on the 65 ter list, and it's 65 ter 3150. With respect to the second request as to admissibility, we do have an objection. First of all, on two grounds, first, that it's simply a commentary on evidence that's already been admitted because it's a compilation or an analysis of that evidence, and we believe the Trial Chamber is better suited to draw its own conclusions. Second, if I could go into private session for one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before we do so. Mr. Waespi, you even introduced the document as 65 ter 3150. That I find that on line -- page 42, line 9. So, therefore, to have it added or did you provisionally assign a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The way I understand it, that's always a technical issue to have it uploaded, so it's everybody -- it's available to everybody. But that doesn't mean that it's formally on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This means that it's your position that it was not yet on a 65 ter list which was filed at the time, and I see some body language on the other side. But whatever it was, either it was or there's no objection against adding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, it is now on the 65 ter list. But now objection against admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could go into private session for one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, had we assigned already a number to this document? Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet. Could you please assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that would be P689.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P689 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In the remaining time, I'd like to cover two more subjects. The first one is Grubori. If the 65 ter number 4817, a sketch, could be pulled up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, do you recognise this sketch?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the sketch, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who prepared it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I drew this sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you fairly briefly, because it's all contained in your various witness statements and specifically in a report you made which is still 65 ter number 5322, can you tell us how come you prepared this sketch.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: This sketch concerns two dates that UN Human Rights Action Team and other personnel went to the Plavno valley north of Knin. The first visit was 24th of August, and we'd gone - if you look at the bottom centre of the diagram, it's the little road coming slightly to the right of centre, it comes from Knin - we'd come that direction, and we'd gone up the road on the left there to the village that's in the top left-hand corner. On the 24th, we had met villagers and they had told us of various incidents of intimidation. They were quite afraid. One building had been burned in that village, and the UN civil affairs and humanitarian officers suggested that to try and take their concerns into consideration, we would come back tomorrow, the next day, with members of the UN -- the Croatian police from Knin to discuss issues such as security, issuing of ID cards, other matters of concern that they expressed to the UN on the 24th. We went back down the road, and we went into Knin, and, as is in my statement, we met briefly at the police station, advised them of the request of the villagers who we'd told the police would come with us on the next day. On the next day, we went to the village again. In my statement, as far as I can recall, we did not go past the Knin police station, but we went directly a bit in advance of the time of that meeting to that village. On the way there, on the road going to the village, you will see these little square boxes on the right-hand side. These were some about 10 to 12 -- 10 to 11 vehicles. Some were blue, some were white kind of vans. And we were somewhat struck, the UN party - which is quite a large one - about these vehicles. They were completely idle and no personnel around, and UN TV crew was with us. They filmed them. I believe you may have that already. I don't know. I took some sketches of the vehicles, and then proceeded up towards the village because we thought they might be to do with the policija from Knin coming to the village. We went to the village top left again, and were told, no, they hadn't come. In the course of that meeting, we observed from that village, across the valley top right, a village that was burning. That is called Grubori, and it's marked top right of that diagram. And the rest is really the roads that we went down past the school community centre and up towards the winding road that goes towards Grubori. I'll leave it there because I think most of the information is in my statement of 1997, specifically my report on the Grubori incident of the 29th of August, which is several pages long, and is there for the Court to consider as to the full account of what I and my colleagues observed first hand in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If this sketch could be admitted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I hear of no objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Exhibit P690.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P690 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could pull up ter 5322.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, is this the report you just referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes. That's my report on the happenings and observations of the UN personnel who went across the Plavno valley to Grubori village on the 25th of August; and in that document, I describe all the events we observed on those days, on the day of the actual incident and the days following.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
