utterances.text: Let me go to page 7, paragraph 27, of this report; and in B/C/S, it's page 9, paragraph 27. The last part of paragraph 27, last five, six lines, read as follows. It starts: "Assessments by UN Sector South, UNCRO, UNHCR, and ECMM that such ongoing incidents, the lack of Croatian police patrols, resources, and investigations, are that they suggest an unchecked pattern that was more toward ethnic cleansing than loose criminal elements and isolated incidents, while balanced reporting by the media is hard to find anywhere in the mainstream Croatian press." Can you tell us the Court why you say that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. As the press and public information officer at Sector South headquarters, I was able to receive reports, not only just the main UN Sector South headquarters, but also the specialised agencies such as UNHCR, which is a UN specialised agency as you know, but also the reports of ECMM monitors that were largely military personnel serving in the European Community Monitoring Mission. And upon reading those in the days after the 4th of August, I can say that every single report from the four principal UN departments, as well as UNHCR, as well as the ECMM, were documenting their own observations of arson in villages, violent acts against what were mainly elderly remaining civilians, and regular observations of what they would describe as men in military uniform or Croatian military officers or special units of Croatia seen at the vicinity of houses o villages that were either on fire, had been burned, or accounts of villagers interviewed. And this is why I say in this paragraph, not that it was in my words "ethnic cleansing," but was an unchecked pattern that continued that was more towards ethnic cleansing than loose criminal elements and isolated incidents. Now, that was what I was reading as reactions by Croatian officials and reported in the Croatian mainstream press which we were monitoring from our press office and was also monitored by our main UN public affairs office in Zagreb. And I did not write that paragraph without some degree of checking with my headquarters in Zagreb because I wanted this report to be, not the most thorough, but as closely to the observations of my colleagues at Grubori, but up to that time of what we observed and I felt were made as genuine reports by the UN officials as well as agencies like UNHCR and ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P691.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P691 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I used my two hours allotted to this witness. I need another maybe ten, 15 minutes, if I'm allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask Madam Registrar how many minutes you exactly used and then please proceed; and if you're well beyond your one and a half hours, then I'll warn you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If 65 ter 4816 could be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this list, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: This is a list that was made, I won't say in a hurried fashion, but was very spontaneous. Because we were puzzled, myself and my UN colleagues, on the way to the village opposite Grubori on the morning of the 25th of August at the sighting of these rather, for us, unusual sight of vehicles parked on the right-hand side of the lane leading towards the village we were going to, after we had come back from the burning ruins of Grubori, I went to check myself with the party vehicles that contained my colleagues. We decided to go to the office of General Cermak to report what we had seen as quickly as possible, and I wanted just to make sure that those vehicles were there or gone. I had recorded on another list, which I could not find, all ten or 11 vehicles on the way to the village we were going to in the morning early. But this is the vehicles that I observed and recorded were still there at the time we returned from Grubori to go to Knin to report what we had seen. It's a very quick note, but it's what I took at the time. And I also have said, I think, in a statement that I believe my colleague -- I believe my colleague from UNHCR, Benny Otim, also took this information on a similar list of the number plates and tablet plates of those vehicles. The sighting itself was quite unusual. They were unmarked, there was no people nearby, it was an open valley, they were quite new vehicles, they looked official. But to me they did not look as if they were Croatian policija vehicles because we were familiar with what they looked like. They looked, as I have said in my report I think, to suggest - and this is in my 1997 statement I think and also my report of 29th August 1995 - that they looked like some kind of special unit vehicles. They were too many to be to be just ordinary normal Croatian policija vehicles. They suggested that type of thing, but that's what I put in my report as my own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P692.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P692 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Waespi, you used approximately one hour, 45 minutes, so if you could please conclude in the next three to four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Brief interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It may be obvious, but if we could just get a date for that document I would appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could you accommodate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, do you remember when you made this note?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yeah, I compiled this note I think the same evening, if not the next day, but I made the actual note at the time, and this I think is the note I took on the 25th of August itself of writing things down. It's clearly a handwritten, hurried note, of the date that is on the top there: Plavno, 25 August 1995. I don't think I wrote it down the next day. I would have remembered the note. I think it is that date or of the evening, but that's the actual list compiled from that sighting late morning, 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I used only -- or if I used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. You said two hours, or you had scheduled two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was one and a half on my mind, so, therefore, I'm not encouraging you to use any more time than you indicated earlier, but my limitation was unfair. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The last photo I'd like to show you in connection to Grubori is 65 ter 4823. Mr. Roberts, can you tell us what -- who the photographer is who took the photograph.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I took this photograph. It was the late afternoon of 25 August. We went back to Grubori, having been in Knin, and reported this development at the office of General Cermak. And this is one of the villagers, Jovo Grubor, who is showing us the location where in the afternoon period while we were in Knin, he had found the body of one of his neighbours in the hedge. And my description of that body and what happened is in my report. Without taking up further time of the Court here, I think that's in the 25 August report of all those photograph I took and what they depict in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I could tender this photo, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Exhibit P693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you invite the witness to be a bit more precise on the time-line that day, at what time approximately he observed initially what he said he observed, then how much time it took him to get back to Knin, and then to get back to Grubori again. Please proceed. Would you please explain this to us, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour. We had gone from the village across from Grubori and reached Grubori about mid-morning, late morning on the 25th. The party of UN officials that were there with myself were UN TV, UNHCR, EJ Flynn from human rights office, about five or six officials including UNCIVPOL and UNMOs. And we spent about, in my opinion, not more than maybe 40 minutes in the village. UN TV filmed. There was a commentary shock on the state of the women and Jovo who came back with us. He was in the meeting across the valley we had been to early in the morning. And we decided then the most important thing to do because of what we had encountered, village houses on fire, barns on fire, cattle, an animal was shot dead, the villagers reporting that some of the relatives were inside houses that were on fire. Clearly, what had happened had obviously for us happened very, very recently, the same hour or two before. We decided to go back to the office of General Cermak and report what we had seen immediately because we felt this warranted a police investigation or security to be provided, and so we went back into Knin which took about 45, 50 minutes. We could not find General Cermak at the office. We spoke to what I think was his -- one of his main assistants, I think Major or General Dondo. My colleagues were Maria Teresa Mauro from UN civil affairs, EJ Flynn, and I think Benny Otim was there from UNHCR. We made it clear to Mr. Dondo what we had seen, where, what we felt was going on, urged an immediate investigation be launched, and the presence of personnel deployed to protect the villagers, not only there but in Plavno valley as we had heard in other incidents like that from other villagers in the morning. We then went back at about 5.00 or so to headquarters Sector South. We tabled very brief, informal initial reports to our respective offices in Zagreb, mission headquarters, and our respective offices elsewhere in the UN chain. Then I had in my office a Dutch TV crew walk in by chance. They were being -- doing some filming elsewhere in the area. And we decided we would go back, those of us who had been there in the morning, to Grubori because we felt the place was very unsecure. We wanted to see if there had been a deployment of Croatian policija to provide security. We went back, we took the Dutch TV crew with us. My colleagues from UN TV decided to stakeout, is the term journalistically, and await the office of General Cermak, to see if they could get an interview with him. We proceeded back to Grubori through Plavno valley, the same route, arriving late afternoon/early evening, and this is when I took most of the photographs of the persons we found had been killed. We were taken to various locations by the villagers, who were by then all assembled, only six remaining, which is I think five women and Jovo here in the photograph. And we were taken to locations where I photographed various people who had been killed in my observations. They had been shot at close range. Bullet cases were found in one room of an elderly man. He was elderly, he'd been in bed. And other women were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you're describing -- I was mainly focusing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's finish up with one subject, and this is 65 ter 2840, a letter from General Janvier to General Cervenko of 12 December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It relates to an issue that you were the -- at the centre of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, if there is one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me read the first one, the third paragraph. "Dear General. "I have been informed by the commander of Sector South, Brigadier-General Forand, that during a visit he paid to General Cermak in Knin on 5 September 1995, General Gotovina, who was also present, accused Mr. Roberts, press and information officer of the Sector, of being involved in spying activities which ultimately may justify his execution." And I'll go on: "You will agree with me that such statements are rude, offending, and unacceptable, especially if expressed by a high-ranking General Officer of the HV. "Moreover, they certainly do not contribute to establishing a very much needed climate of cooperation and confidence at a time where reports on looting, burning, and other human rights violations continue to reach me and the Commander of Sector South. "I would very much appreciate it if you could inform me about whatever measures you deem necessary to avoid further blatant allegations against a member of the UN in Sector South whose commitment remains highly valued by the Sector Commander." Now, were you spying, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, I don't even know these days where that question comes from, but I was a professional public information officer of UN Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what the reason was that General Gotovina used these words or acted the way he did?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the question calls for speculation. The person wasn't even at the meeting, so I don't know if he can even accurately -- he's basically asking him to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it calls for speculation depends on what he knows. But, Mr. Waespi, you certainly have an expectation, I take it, that if we start digging into the psychology of Mr. Gotovina at the time, then it might not greatly assist us. But if the witness has any specific knowledge which could give a reasonable explanation for why he was perceived as being a spy, then, of course, the witness could tell us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you're asking me to comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Actually, what we'd like to know is what facts you are aware of which you could link to such an allegation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there's a few things here, begging the Court's indulgence. I was not present at the meeting at all. I was advised by General Forand, the sector commander, that he had been invited to a meeting, which, in fact, as far as I understand, was a meeting or an invitation extended by General Gotovina, not by General Cermak, to his headquarters or winter headquarters, as General Forand told me in Knin. They went. That's all I knew. I didn't ask to go, I was not invited to go. When General Forand returned, I was called by Colonel Tymchuk, one of his advisors, to his office where I was briefed that in the course of that meeting, there was two things that seemed especially, to put it politely, very much on the mind of General Gotovina as described to me by General Forand, which was that we and the UNHCR were harbouring war criminals in Sector South that we should hand over. First of all, that's what I was told. And, secondly, he seemed especially disturbed with my behaviour and made, as I was told by General Forand, by Colonel Tymchuk, in the presence of several officers accompanying General Forand, a threat against myself personally with several allegations that I was an agent, provacateur, et cetera. I was only asked for my comment about how I felt. I cautioned by my colleagues that I did not myself feel any kind of sense of foreboding threat on the streets of Knin, that I was doing my job. If General Forand felt that was reliable, I would continue; and, therefore, the Sector South commander placed this at the latter part of his report to Zagreb, but advised me he must tell UN officials of this threat. If something happened, he and other UN officials in Zagreb would be liable. I then saw the rest of the correspondence from the force commander to higher UN -- higher Croatian military officials. I did see the response of General Gotovina. As I told you, I was not at the meeting. I can myself offer you, if you wish to have it, my -- what would be correctly speculation as to why he may have said this, but I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not invited to give any explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you read the whole of the letter. We heard quite a long answer, which finally doesn't bring us what we asked for; that is, whether there are any specific facts. The only thing I heard is that, apparently, Mr. Gotovina has expressed that he considered Mr. Roberts to be an agente provocateur, well, which is, of course, not exactly the same thing as a spy, but that's the only thing that's added.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps one last question which focuses on the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We know from your witness statements which are now in evidence that you had a number of meetings with General Gotovina prior to the Operation Storm. Now, given those meetings, does this reaction of General Gotovina, who, as we read, wanted to say that it justifies your execution, did that come as a surprise to you?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I did not have meetings myself, my initiation, with General Gotovina. I was in the presence of UN sector commanders. I felt at those meetings that he had expressed more than once that, as the UN public information officer, he felt the messages I was portraying and saying to the press, especially in Zadar and Croatia and in Korenica, were not appropriate. And I felt he was quite upset with what he and his colleagues were monitoring what I was saying. And I knew he did not like the role of myself and other UN colleagues in the way we were acting inside Sector South in performing our mandate. That was made very clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The letter, which apparently is page 2 of this -- I'll just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I've seen the letter before, but apparently in the first page is now the -- it is a 12th of September message from UNCRO COS, apparently to commander Sector South Alun Roberts, subject: "Threat against the Sector South spokesman by HV authorities."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It might well be that another version came in with General Forand. I need to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But just for the sake of completion, I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could we then at least understand that you received a copy of this correspondence, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have -- I did have at the time the sitrep that went from Sector South commander to headquarters, and I have received subsequently the response of General Janvier at the time, more or less, and subsequently the correspondence between Mr. Janvier and Croatian senior officials later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, we'll hear from you whether you insist on having this in evidence, which might be repetitious evidence, but I have not verified that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Who will be the first one to cross-examine the witness? Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're on your feet. Mr. Roberts, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay, who is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just on a general notice, Your Honour will recollect, and I think it's proper for me to this point out, the error that General Forand spoke of in relation to this particular letter that there wasn't a meeting at General Cermak's office. General Cermak wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, the first matter I want to deal with is your initial meetings referred to in your statement with no clear date, but you state in those statements that you were present at meetings either on the 7th or 8th of August at General Cermak's office in which matters such as freedom of movement were discussed. And I'll suspect you'll probably remember those details. We've no need to look at them on the screen because I'm going to refer you to various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For the Court's assistance, we'll be dealing with evidence that arises in the statement of August 1997, Exhibit P675, para 20; the statement of 28th of February, 2007, Exhibit P677. And it concerns the details that arise from that passage within those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your first meeting, then, Mr. Roberts, outside the UNCRO camp was when?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Thank you. My first meeting with General Cermak was in the presence of the sector commander on the morning or late morning of the 8th of August, as I recall to the best of my ability and as I've put in the statement. That was the meeting that General Forand had requested to discuss a number of matters, and a number of us went from headquarters Sector South to meet General Forand in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to that meeting, within those statements, you give characterization as to the role of Mr. Cermak and what was allegedly said by him; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: That is generally correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving back a day to the 7th of August, that was a day when Mr. Akashi came to the camp; and, presumably, on that day, that was the first day that you met General Cermak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Not exactly. On the 7th of August was the visit, as you explained, by the SRSG, Mr. Akashi. After he had toured the town of Knin which was supervised very much by the Croatian authorities, naturally, he came to the Sector South headquarters. And I don't know whether he was accompanied by General Cermak or not, but there was a press briefing. Now, my only contact with General Cermak was that he was sitting and seated on the right-hand side of Mr. Akashi. I did not meet with him. I arranged the room with my other colleagues from the press office for the press conference. I did not speak to him directly, and later in the same statement, I've recorded the press conference and main remarks by some journalists in questions to Mr. Akashi and Mr. Cermak. I did not meet him on the 7th of August in any kind of conversational way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 7th of August, then, was the first day that you had any contact with him in that sense, in the sense of seeing him?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: That's very correct. That's very fair. It's the first time I'd seen General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your statements, you're unclear as to the date when there was a meeting concerning the discussions of the UNCRO contingent and discussions with General Cermak over where they could or could not go. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I think, to the best of my ability, that the first two statements I actually made to ICTY investigators in 1997/1998 were perhaps the clearest. And I, in 1997 in that paragraph 20, recall the meeting of UNCRO officials from Sector South headquarters with General Cermak. That is a description. There is nothing there in quotation marks. It is my observations as to the kind of meeting we had, what General Forand wished to try and accomplish, and the characterization of the response of General Cermak of what he replied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in your statement of 2007, you say it was either one or the other date, and I'm looking at page 7 of that statement and the second paragraph: "I recall that either Monday, the 7th, or Tuesday, the 8th of August, I went with General Forand and other UN officials to meet with General Cermak."

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why the uncertainty?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: At the time of this statement, if you look at the date, it is 2007. And as a small aside, it's a long time between the statement to an investigator of, I think, early 1997 - in fact, August 1997 - to what is, in fact, ten years after, 2007, which in some parts might have been just generally descriptive. But I, having reviewed the 1997 statement, recall that the meeting, in fact, was the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the 7th of August, when General Cermak was at the UNCRO camp and after Mr. Akashi had gone, were you present when there was a meeting between him and members of the displaced persons who were present at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I don't think on that occasion I was present, but I was present, I think, at a later meeting, or I thought was later, in which General Cermak spoke to a delegation of the displaced persons. I cannot recall being at a meeting on the 7th of August, but I know that General Cermak had expressed his wish to meet with the displaced persons as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I might be wrong about that date. I'm trying to position you to help you, as there's uncertainty about it. And for these questions, that's not really important. It may, in fact. Have been on the 8th of August, you're quite right. So you weren't present on the 7th of August when General Forand met General Cermak at General Cermak's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I just heard you say the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I was not at a meeting that I recall was on the 7th of August. I recall that Mr. Akashi was in town on the 7th of August, and there was a press briefing late that morning, and that General Cermak attended the press briefing. I can recall going to a meeting with General Forand and the head of civil affairs, Mr. Al-Alfi, and other heads of the UN, which I had thought was the 8th of August, and that's why I put it in my statement of 1997, that I recall that meeting of a large delegation of the UN as being the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we turn to Exhibit P356, please. This is a sitrep dated the 8th of August. Can we turn to page 2 of that UNCRO sitrep and go to paragraph 8 if that can be blown up for the benefit of -- or raised up the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in paragraph 8, we see here from this document from HQ Sector South Knin, presumably this is a document that you would have seen, is that right? It's an UNCRO sitrep.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I can't recall seeing this document previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So are we to take it that not all UNCRO sitreps actually came before you?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: The majority of them did, I had access to all of them, but I can't recall the specificity of this document on the meeting of the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us at all as to what types of UNCRO sitreps that were being transmitted to Zagreb didn't go to you?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I had access to most of the documentation that went from Sector South commander's office to Zagreb, as well as UNMOs and UNCIVPOL and UN Human Rights Action Team reports penned by the heads of that departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm asking you about UNCRO sitreps because that's what we've got in front of us, and I would be grateful if you would direct your attention to that because you said most of documents. I'd like to know if there was a category that didn't, if you were excluded from any particular acquire of document?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: If they were confidential memoirs between the sector commander and of a military nature with headquarters or perhaps something from UNCRO, head of political affairs that were thought sensitive, we would not necessarily get them. We can't say every single specific document, but the majority, yes, I would have access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning, then, to paragraph 8, this is a report of the meeting written here with the commander of Sector South, General Forand, General Cermak, and you can see that the meeting refers to one that took place at 6.00 on the 7th of August to discuss items of mutual interest. It refers to who was assisting General Forand, CAC. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: It would be the civil affairs coordinator. I think it's not quite the right terminology for the exact title of the post of Mr. Hussein Al-Alfi, but, you're right, basically that's who it would be. Senior Military Observer, EJ Flynn, head of the human rights section --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: SMO, senior monitoring officer?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Senior military observer, I think is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: DEPCOMD?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Deputy commander, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would that have been Mr. Tymchuk or Mr. Leslie?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Andrew Leslie, I think, at the time was the Chief of Staff who departed shortly after to Zagreb. That's not as I had understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the SLO, that's senior liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Senior liaison officer, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, there, General Cermak was assisted by a Captain Lukovic?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The tone of meeting cordial, atmosphere within the HQ was with intense activity, which left the impression the HV was unprepared for its success.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I haven't got that in front of me. Could you turn the page or pull that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Military governor expressed a desire for frequent meetings, even daily, and he asked to visit and speak to the displaced population - internally displaced persons population is what that stands for - at the headquarters in Sector South on the 8th of August. This was agreed. UN humanitarian agencies must soon decide the criteria concerning questioning of the IDPs. A paragraph concerning the civil authorities, a paragraph concerning observation posts, patrolling would now be done by UNCIVPOL and other UN teams that you're familiar with, about the agreement between the Government of Croatia and UNCRO. Concern about -- or the initial area considered safe for travel by the Croatian authorities is the area of Knin. This will be progressively expanded. Further references there. It was agreed UNHCR convoys would be free to travel within the area and that storage space would be made available for supplies in Knin, and then special measures concerning protection of people. So that was the position as recorded by General Forand's staff, and we've heard evidence about that from him, on the 7th of August, and the discussion there with General Cermak concerning freedom of movement. And you weren't present at that meeting, as we know.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me just be very clear with you. It may be a different date of one day. I was in the party with General Forand, with EJ Flynn, with Benny Otim, with Mr. Al-Alfi, that met with Mr. Cermak in his office in the centre of town. This sitrep I'm reading, for me, for me, what is very important, even if with the Court's forgiveness it is a matter of one day, is what was said at that meeting. I'm reading this sitrep very carefully; and as I do, I recall seeing some of this before. But I recall very, very certainly contact with General Forand, Benny Otim of UNHCR, before we had that meeting with General Cermak. And the biggest concern, the biggest concern, was of the UN's ability to get out of Sector South headquarters, patrol the streets of Knin, and get out to verify what might be happening, might be happening, in the villages, hamlets around, as per UNCRO full freedom of movement. And what I've said there on that paragraph is exactly as I remember, General Forand being quite strong, polite, in his request that we be allowed to do that, and saying very clearly, If you do not allow us to do this, if you do not allow us to do this, I cannot say that Croatian authorities, political military police are standing by human rights. Now, that's my version of what I distinctly remember being said by the sector commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you earlier read or summarized this document, and the line that the HV "seemed not to be prepared for success" is not the same as that they "seemed at least slightly unprepared for the rapid success." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, can I say, I only did that to skip through quickly. There's nothing in this line of questioning to do with that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I am concerned, and I do invite you to look at it very carefully, Mr. Roberts, is that your characterization within your statements of your meetings with General Cermak at a meeting with Mr. Forand are not as borne-out by what is written in your statement. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I'm looking here at one document that you have shown about that meeting. I also had seen summary reports of that meeting from my colleague EJ Flynn and from civil affairs. I have not tendered them as part of my supporting evidence, but I think that there definitely was discussion, as I recall other sitreps of the sector commander's office, specifically in regard to that meeting, pointing out what was agreed at that meeting of freedom of movement, and that it was not being followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you because your evidence was quite clear in those statements, which you've told us was the truth, was that General Cermak was restricting you to the centre of town and just side-streets. This is not reflected in this document, is it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying clearly what I heard, first of all, and recall at that meeting. And I do know, sir, that there are other documents from the office of General Forand and from UNMOs and CIVPOL in the days immediately following that meeting, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. We're talking about your characterization of General Cermak at the meeting where you give an impression of who he was and what he was. Please do not move to further down what was happening later. Please deal with the accuracy of what you were asked to give evidence about.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: And my response, then, is that what I put in this document is what I recall, to the best of my ability, the statements of General Forand at that time and the responses that we understood from General Cermak on his authority and what he said in terms of his ability: We should have freedom of movement in the centre and side-streets of Knin to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking at this document, and you've told us you've seen many of them, is there any reference to you -- other than it being distributed to you internally, is there any reference to you being present at this meeting on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: No. I do not see anything referring to me being present at that meeting, described as happening on the 7th of August. However, I am in the court under oath, and I was at a meeting attended by General Forand, with Hussein Al-Alfi from civil affairs, EJ Flynn, Benny Otim, in the office of General Forand, General Cermak, as I recall in my statement, on the 8th of August. You're pointing out the sitrep of the 7th, and I've said what was for me very significant at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we, then, move to another document dated the 7thof August, Exhibit P111.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're going to look at another document now, another UNMO HQ Sector South daily sitrep, dealing with what happened on that day, released by Mr. Ermolaev. And we can see the first page there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us now turn to page 7, a summary of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You'll see a time there in August, UN special representative Mr. Akashi had a meeting. You'll see in the next section a Sector South delegation, including DSMO.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I'm not seeing that. It needs to go down, if it could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Met in former ARSK HQ with newly posted military governor of Knin. So it's another report of the same meeting, and you referred to there being other reports. General Cermak and senior Croatian army liaison officer, Sector South delegation was told, UNMOs, CIVPOL, and other humanitarian would be able to monitor within Knin town boundaries and other areas, but on the 8th of August, afternoon, Sector South would receive info about the areas where security of UNMOs and other humanitarian agencies - turning to next page - cannot be guaranteed. Sector South delegation told: Military and CIVPOL ... took over control of Knin. The next matter, the new military governor stated they will try to re-establish electricity. The next matter, General Cermak expressed his desire to meet with refugees, and there was to be a meeting on the 8th of August. So just turning back to that page 7, which is the relevant matter on this issue, would you agree this description is different from the description given by you in your statement that at a meeting, General Cermak was restricting the UN to the town centre and side-streets?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I think that this document is an interpretation, but I can recall what was said. Here, if you look at the last few lines that: "CIVPOL and other humanitarian would be able to monitor within Knin town bounders and other areas. But on the 8th of August afternoon, Sector South would receive information about the areas where security of UNMOs and other humanitarian agencies can ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "... not be guaranteed," is where it moves on to on the next page.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Right. Well, I can recall at that same meeting that I have referred to in my report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yours isn't a report; it's a statement.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: But, nevertheless, sir, it was a document that was in other ways passed on to my public information office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have contemporaneous notes of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I think I may have, but I don't know whether I have them now. But I think that I recall having some of the meeting when I compiled some of this in 1997, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Roberts, to make it clear, contemporaneous means at the time, not what you write a couple of years later.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. But do you have any notes at the time, written at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I do not recall I took notes of that meeting at that very time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes. I was present at a meeting with General Forand, General Cermak in the centre of Knin, and I've said that now three times. And I was there and my colleagues who also were there would know I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything else you would like to say, then, about the --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Can I just see the very first page of this sitrep that you brought up, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 1.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: The very front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Not that I'm saying I saw anything, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For internal distribution PIO.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: That's right, yeah. Just on that last paragraph: Croatian authorities stated that restriction for UNMOs and other humanitarian organizations will be lifted on the 8th of August, but there will be some areas where security cannot be guaranteed." May I for the court and for reference, my collection on that - I don't know what has been said by other witnesses who may have been before the Tribunal - again, I politely insist that I recall the sector commander saying to General Cermak that the UN had the ability to decide what were secure areas and what were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's now turn to Exhibit page 3 -- Exhibit Prosecution 359. Your Honour, actually looking at the time, we're going into the matters on that day. It may be better to take the second break at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll now take a break and we'll resume at a quarter to 1.00, so that we then have one hour still available today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Exhibit P359, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a Sector South report again for the next day, the 8th of August, distributed internally to you, Mr. Roberts. If we turn to page 2 we see in commander's assessment that there was two meetings on this day, one with Mr. Gotovina and one where Mr. Cermak. And we're going to look at the report of those meetings. If we turn to page 3 of the document, the meeting with Mr. Gotovina was in the Knin fortress, and you've referred to that as a meeting of which you were aware. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of that meeting that Sector South commander went to. I think it was the meeting that President Tudjman came to the fortress, and it was that meeting that General Forand went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: If this is the meeting that was at the fortress, on the evening I think of the 6th of August, I was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. This is at 9.20 on the 8th of August, 9.20 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: No. I was not at that meeting in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And you can see in this report here that the meeting with General Gotovina between General Forand, General Forand refers to having met General Cermak previously, and that's the previous day. And then you'll see, in part 2, that freedom of movement is discussed with General Gotovina. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is this a sitrep that you read at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I recall, if not seeing this document, something very similar to it, in regard to the issue of freedom of movement being set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Court --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I'm looking at paragraph 3. Just one moment if I could. Some of this I can recall, but not very clearly in terms of it being like yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. You'll see in the third paragraph, as numbered on that page, a meeting between General Forand and Mr. Cermak; and paragraph 1 of that document, you'll see, recounts Colonel Cermak, it says this, coming to HQ Sector South at 1.00 to meet with General Forand and a committee of IDPs. Now, that's the 8th of August. Were you present when General Cermak met the IDPs that afternoon at the UNCRO camp?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I can't be sure right now that it was that meeting, but there was a meeting certainly near the front gate of the Sector South camp one afternoon. I think I've put it in one of my statements it was later, but it could have been the 8th of August. If that was so and it was the front gate at a table with chairs and so on, I was sitting at that table, and General Cermak did address the -- what was a delegation of representatives of the IDPs that had been established. I thought that took place later because that kind of discussion on whether they could have been representation I think took some days, but I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You'll see in this subparagraph 1, of what's numbered 3 there at the bottom, that General Cermak's referred to being a very busy man, he was soon to go to his headquarters, he would give orders that UN elements would be allowed to travel freely within Knin and to Drnis, something he had been prevented from doing until now due to the pressure of his schedule. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I do see what it says there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you agree that the UNCRO report here recording what was said reflects no restrictions to there being restricted movement within Knin itself?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I can see what it says, but I'm also recalling quite vividly the internal discussions we had, and I do not think it was so easy that we had freedom of movement or we moved around so quickly unrestricted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why I'm asking these questions is your characterization in your statement of 2007, February 2007, at page 7, that Cermak eventually agreed to let the UN patrol the main street and the centre part of the town from the 8th of August, as though he'd been the subject of considerable pressure by General Forand and he eventually gave a concession. That was not the case, was it, Mr. Roberts?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, I'm very sorry, but I have to disagree with you. I recall, before we'd even met with General Cermak, the very strong feelings of General Forand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there. It's not general strong feelings about anyone. You're not here giving a press conference of inaccurate information or summaries by you; it's exactly what was said that we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the witness should be allowed to explain. If counsel puts to him that he cannot -- wasn't honest or something, I think he should be at least given the chance to finish his sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just read again what Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't want my time to be lost, Your Honour, by unfocused answers not addressing the issue, and that's the submission I make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness only started his answer and may finish his answer. At the same time, Mr. Roberts, you're invited to answer as concisely as possible mainly about facts, not about general impressions, unless there are certain facts that led you to have these impressions. The last question was: Mr. Kay put it to you that it was not the case that Mr. Cermak eventually agreed to let the UN patrol the main street and the centre part of the town, only being subject of considerable pressure by General Forand. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do think there was a very strong conversation that I recall taking place, not a long one, not a long one, but I recall clearly the statement at the meeting of General Cermak, that it was not completely secure for the UN to have freedom of movement in all of Knin. And I recall the response of General Forand being, more or less, Thank you, sir, but the UN will have to decide what is secure and what is not. We wish to have as soon as possible - I recall that, more or less, being said - freedom of movement in and around Knin and also to determine that for ourselves. And that was a kind of loggerhead point; and at the end of the meeting it was, Very well. Okay. You've got the centre of Knin and the side-streets. And, again, the issue came from General Cermak that it wasn't completely secure, and he couldn't give consent beyond Knin. That is my very clear recollection of that meeting and very polite assistance of General Alain Forand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You weren't at this meeting on the 8th of August, is that right, at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: This meeting at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: As I've said earlier, I recall there being a meeting with the DPs and attended by General Cermak. I can't be sure it's this early on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. It's at the meeting with General Forand and General Cermak at the camp.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: No, I was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A meeting with the displaced persons is something entirely different.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Right. I was not at that meeting with General Forand and General Cermak at the camp together with the DPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that General Gotovina had supplied a map on the 8th of August to General Forand, showing the areas that could be used for travel?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I see paragraph 2 here, and I recall at the time being told of a discussion where maps would be produced by the Croatian military in regard to where we could patrol and move and where we could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know where that was produced from? Did you know it was General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I did not know General Gotovina personally, if that's what you're saying. I understood it was from the Croatian military that maps would be produced in regard to where we could go and did not go. I'm looking here, if I may, sir, at paragraph 2. It does not, to my mind, record a response or any real characterization of the issue of freedom of movement. It just says what General Gotovina had said he would do, in regard to my interpretation there, we can go certain places, but maps would define where we could go and where we could not. That's not full freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I'm challenging -- Mr. Roberts, you've made statements you've told the Court are the truth; and in those statements, you gave your opinion that you assumed the desire of General Cermak to limit UN access only to the centre of town was because this would allow further clean-up in the streets and side roads away from the town centre without UN personnel having access to see the real situation and what was happening. That's what I'm addressing these questions to you --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I understand completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- because you insinuate in that part of your statement that General Cermak was trying to restrict movement around Knin so that crimes could be committed. That was the purpose of you putting that in your statement, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I've heard you just say now so that crimes can be committed. I have not said that. I have the distinct impression of myself, my observations, and those of my colleagues of there being restrictions of movement in the early days after Knin fell, and the conclusion was because clean-up was certainly going on in a very, very quick and vigorous and organized way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Because when we got out into town, we were seeing that places that my colleagues and myself had seen on the 4th of August and others had seen them on the 5th of August, glass windows of shops that had been damaged replaced very, very quickly; other repairs going on to certain places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What's wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Just in terms of things being organized, as if in advance, to put things together, and just in terms of what my colleagues had seen, and in terms of the shelling on the 4th of August. Traces of that were not observed in the early part when we get out, and that was several days after. My colleagues --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, you move things further and further away from the question. What you said in this statement here was: " ... to see the real situation and what was happening."

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What did you mean by that in your statement if you weren't trying to insinuate that General Cermak was restricting movement within Knin so that crimes could be committed?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: You are saying crimes could be committed. I've never said that in a statement. You're referring that I have said that and I have never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "real situation"?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the fact of the UN's desire from the evening of the 5th of August to get out into Knin to verify what was happening in town, and that we were restricted on that late afternoon by an APC, being blocked, and we did not get out into town with any proper authority to patrol regularly until the early part of the 8th of August. And, therefore, I am saying we could not see what was going on, but certainly a clean-up was going on and we were not able to verify to say what did or did not take place. I know very well that not only for myself, my colleagues have also expressed the same opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at Exhibit P513, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the document referred to on the 8th of August in that sitrep which was the document promised to General Forand by General Cermak, and you'll notice here the terms of that document. "As of 8th of August, all UNCRO elements with clearly displayed insignia may move freely in the areas of Knin and Drnis. "Advise them to use main roads only. If they're turning off them, it is at their own risk ..." You would agree, there, nothing about restricting people to the centre of Knin and the side-streets?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I see what's written there is reference to "move freely in the areas," areas, "of Knin and Drnis. "2. Advise them to use main roads only," only main roads. "If they're turning off them, it is at their own risk ..." I do not see there, sir, a clear reference to full freedom of movement. I see paragraph 2 being an interpretation of what might be restriction of UN movement to only main roads. We did not ask for that. And Knin and Drnis, does this mean though we could move along the road from Knin to Drnis, roads off Drnis, roads off Knin? Those are occasions I know my colleagues have reported, restrictions of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm asking you for your evidence, and can you explain why your statement about what was the permission given to the UN, why it is different from what was actually happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, what I'm looking at, sir, is a letter. What is actually happening on the ground as borne-out by my colleagues - and I don't know if they testified or not - but from their reports is what I was going on. And there was clear evidence in reality of restrictions of movement to UN personnel, despite this particular letter. And if I may, with due respect to the Court, I know very well from seeing the letters that General Forand politely sent to General Cermak letters protesting restrictions of movement on no less than six or seven occasions. Those letters have passed to me. I did not use them in any way before the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, you talk about other things happening later, and I'm asking you to focus on what you have said was happening on the 7th or 8th of August, not what was happening days later and what was happening on the ground, but acts and conduct that you ascribe to General Cermak, not other things. Can we get that clear?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we are very clear, or at least I am very clear. I am very clear what was said in the meeting with General Cermak, what was advised to him -- the meeting with General Forand, sorry, advised to him by General Cermak. And I am very clear what I saw and my colleagues saw in those same days in reality, and the two things are not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move on to a new matter, and that concerns General Cermak's appointment. Did you know he was a civilian immediately prior to the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Not at the time, no. "Not at the time," I mean not at the time we were introduced to him as the military commander of Knin. I believe the right terminology is garrison commander, but I learned that later. But I didn't know he had been in civilian life previously, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you seen in the press an article in Slobodna Dalmacija, dated the 6th of August, 1995, about his appointment as commander of the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I can't recall it being in Slobodna Dalmacija, but I recall our press office monitoring the press at that time and reading that General Cermak had been appointed to that post with that form of title, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For the Court purposes, we've seen the newspaper report at Exhibit D36. I won't call that up now. Can we produce Exhibit D37.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your press office monitored the Croatian press; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. I think all UN missions have media monitoring units, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this article in Slobodna Dalmacija, dated the 10th of August, 1995, is an interview with General Cermak about the restoration of Knin and the surrounding area. Was this an article that you would have seen at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I can't recall now that we saw that article and translated it. I'll explain very briefly. We didn't have access to Croatian newspapers in the normal way we had previously in the days following Operation Storm. So I recall the general context of it, but not necessarily that we transcribed that newspaper article at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the statements as in this article, about the task of General Cermak: "We are in the process of restoring the Knin Garrison. We are doing our best to bring normality back to a town with no civilian authorities, no water, electricity, or telephone lines." Were you aware of that as being his task?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: You're telling me that's his task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Is that from the newspaper report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: -- itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, it's an interview with him.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I'd be very careful. I respect very well the description of General Cermak himself and his authorities, but I don't know precisely what was the official authorities -- that explains one function of work. "We are doing our best," where "we" I would suppose being the Croatian authorities, and an interpretation of his: "A town with no civilian authorities," yes, "no water," which is a very general description of what his -- some of his duties might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I was not aware that that officially was his sole responsibility - not that I'm suggesting it is - but I'm not -- if you're saying that was his function --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You're not here to suggest anything, just to give us what you knew.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me what I'm seeing in the quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay, if you're saying that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I take the point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- this was his function, then the witness as a matter of fact asks, seeks clarification of your question, so that he's fully entitled to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to add anything else? I wouldn't like to cut you off, Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: It's okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Clearly, the town, in the days following Operation Storm, yes, these things were a problem, as I recollect, for UN Sector South headquarters: Lack of electricity, supply being regular, water-supply was off for, I think, a day. Yes. Those things were a good characterization here as presented by General Cermak in his quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: D38, please, Exhibit D38.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is from Vecernji List that we're going to look at in a moment, another newspaper, 11th of August, 1995, where the task of General Cermak is set out in paragraph 2 in the English. "My task is to coordinate the establishment of civilian authority ... running of all systems necessary for a normal life of the town. That includes coordinating the work of the civilian police, the military police, and the civilian authority. Currently, there is no civilian authority in Knin. The government has appointed its commissioner Petar Pasic ..." And we can see the rest of the text. Again, a report you would have seen at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I think I recall, sir, not exactly the time the newspaper was published, but I think we had a copy of that within a few days, and I'm not sure it was translated at the time, but I remember being told and then a rough-hand translation was made of some of these extracts that you've pointed out here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: -- in terms of especially the one where General Cermak is saying, "My task is to coordinate, as this is before us here."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many meetings were you at where General Cermak was present?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I was present at not very many meetings. The meeting of the 8th of August, as I recall, with the main UN officials. There was, I think, one or two other meetings I attended with EJ Flynn and Mr. Hussein Al-Alfi later on in regard to human rights and humanitarian matters. And there was a meeting I was present at, as I explained, where General Cermak did address a delegation of DPs I felt later in the week of the 8th of August, some weeks further on, I think, just inside the gates of Sector South. And that was about it in terms of my being at meetings rather than having meetings with, if I can put it like that. Then the last one was perhaps was the evening of the big bus convoy leaving Sector South headquarters to go across to Serbia with the DPs in the camp, where there was a group of male persons who were identified as allegedly having committed war crimes, and we talked very briefly at the gate that night. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the tasks that he was to deal with, you didn't know anything about the Croatian government system as to why he was there and what powers he had from them. You didn't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I did not. I recall, sir, that I had asked my press office in Zagreb mission headquarters just for information: Did they have a document, official or otherwise, in terms of the right title of General Cermak, his terms of reference as set out by the Croatian government authorities who appointed him. I did not get anything like that from my press office, so I was not clear in terms of what was the official exact terminology of the Croatian government defined for General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll look at Exhibit D36, then, which is another passage from Slobodna Dalmacija on the 6th of August, 1995, the day after his appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's headed --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Could I just -- sorry. Is it allowable for me to make a comment on this article that's before us already in Slobodna Dalmacija that's quoted by General Cermak or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If at the end of your testimony you would like to add anything you consider relevant and if you make a note of that so as to remember, that's fine, but not during the examination by Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- unless it becomes relevant in relation to one of the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This was the report of Slobodna Dalmacija of the appointment that was made the previous day, the 5th of August, and you can see the Croatian newspaper piece there and the translation on the left of the screen. Was this a document that you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I recall seeing this maybe at least over a week or maybe two weeks after it was published. There were, I think, one or two other similar ones in other mainstream Croatian press based upon, you can see here, it says Zagreb HINA. HINA is the Croatian press agency. But I go with that. So I can recall reading a week or two after the actual publication of the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And within the structure that -- sorry, within the structure of the Croatian armed forces, the position of commander of Knin garrison, was that something you researched or someone informed you about at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I recall - being careful that I'm not stepping out of the direct question - but I recall discussion at Sector South headquarters about the terms of reference of General Cermak. I don't want to say anything further in case I'm not answering the question. But I see here and I remember seeing at the time, these were set out to be, according to HINA, the Croatian press agency, his duties and tasks as commander of the Knin garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: It's like a biography.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's released the next day. In terms of what you knew, he said he was there to assist the UN in Sector South; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: That's what I really recall General Cermak saying in a very - I can say this - in a sense of cooperation, that he portrayed in words that if there should be difficulties, problems, freedom of movement, humanitarian issues, without him actually saying those words, that we should come to him, that he should be the person we have in our mind as the main interlocutor in Knin. And that's why, I think, my colleagues who, because of their specific mandates, had meetings with him more regular than I did, people like the sector commander, Mr. Al-Alfi, civil affairs, EJ Flynn, Benny Otim, and so on. But he, General Cermak, was the person that they would go and meet with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And as you said, you were only at a few meetings on other matters, but were you aware that his role in relation to the internally displaced persons in the camp was to help UNCRO try and solve that problem on its door-step?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: He was, yes, the main interlocutor on behalf of the Croatian government authorities that General Forand had meetings with on that particular issue of the DPs. General Forand was also at times accompanied at times, I understand, by people such as the head of UN civil affairs because it was a political civilian matter as well. But that was our main interlocutor. General Forand, too, General Cermak at the Sector South level in Knin; and to their counterpart separate headquarters UN, and I suppose to the Croatian government through the command of General Cermak, on which there were many, many discussions about that particular problem that you've highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Court has seen a vast raft of documents solely on those issues.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I don't propose to go through those in the interests of time, as it was only a few weeks ago. Even if it had been months ago, I know the Court would know the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you described General Forand reporting, did you mean to UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: On the issue of the DPs, or on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes. That was a very sensitive matter for a range of reasons, notwithstanding the fact of the quite strong, understandable, but strong insistence on the Croatian authorities of there being suspected war criminals amongst the DPs that they wished to interview, and there was many discussions on that aspect before it was finally resolved. I think the Court probably knows the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You refer in your statement to the people who were eventually separated from the main group of people who were to be allowed out of the camp to go to Serbia or Bosnia, wherever it was, that they eventually went; that there was a number, 35 in fact, who were retained under the authority of the Croatian government for questioning in relation to suspected war crimes. You were aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I think it was very well documented. I have referred to it, I think, in my 1997 statement. Yes, in simplified terms, although it was a very big issue. When you say "separate," it was that evening, basically, that we had resolved over a period of a week or more with the assistance of a UN - I won't say certified - but UN-blessed Croatian advocate, a woman lawyer, to come into the Sector South camp to interview what was a much reduced list of male persons in the DP community, in the camp, to meet with them, to discuss with them. And we got - we didn't get - but the list came down to about 34, 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have seen all this evidence --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- yet.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Well, the evening concerned they were put on buses outside the Sector South headquarters first and driven away to respective detention centres, I think, in Split, Zadar, elsewhere, Sibenik; and then, after that, the DPs some hours later were put on other buses, many buses, to go across to Serbia and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you're critical of General Cermak being present when Croatian authorities were filming these suspects leaving the camp, and you say you became involved in a way by then filming the Croatian TV or reporters who were recording the matter. And you were critical of General Cermak in respect of that. Do you recollect that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I recollect it very well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking at that, do you think what you were doing, was in fact, being provocative by filming Croatian authorities filming people who had not been in their custody or authority, but were coming out of the UN and coming into the authority of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: You are asking if you think I personally was not being provocative?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that you were being provocative by then filming the filmers.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's at paragraphs 29 to 33 --

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- of you're August 1997 statement.

utterances.speaker: ALUN ROBERTS
utterances.text: First of all, to try and summarize this for the Court, this was a very difficult evening, a long evening, at the end of a lot of negotiation by senior UN officials in Zagreb headquarters, one of two of which were deployed to Sector South to assist this whole process of the handing over of those suspected of committing war crimes to the Croatian authorities and the others a few hours later to be bussed out to respective communities or whatever through Republic of Croatia to Serbia. On that evening - without going away from your question, but just for a slight moment - there was discussion of adding on additional numbers of males to the agreed 34, I think. That's a side issue. But as they were going out, the males who were the alleged war crimes suspects, quite rightly being handed over to the Croatian authorities to face the evidence against them, I was quite astonished that the TV unit came forward and filmed them very close up, face-on, as they went into the doors of the buses. I talked to EJ Flynn. We had the UN TV crew inside the gates, and I decided to go with EJ, who as I understood it made representation to General Cermak that this is not very helpful, polite.
